t:
(a) Consolidation.—Subsection (a) of section 2668 of title 10, United States Code, is amended—
        (1) in the matter preceding paragraph (1)—
            (A) by striking “he” both places it appears and inserting “the Secretary”; and 
            (B) by striking “his control, to a State, Commonwealth, or possession, or political subdivision thereof, or to a citizen, association, partnership, or corporation of a State, Commonwealth, or possession,” and inserting “the Secretary’s control”;  
        (2) in paragraph (2), by striking “oil pipe lines” and inserting “gas, water, sewer, and oil pipe lines”; and 
        (3) in paragraph (13), by striking “he considers advisable, except a purpose covered by section 2669 of this title” and inserting “the Secretary considers advisable”.  
    (b) Stylistic Amendments.—Such section is further amended—
        (1) in subsection (a), by inserting “Authorized Types of Easements.—” after “(a)”; 
        (2) in subsection (b), by inserting “Limitation on Size of Easement.—” after “(b)”; 
        (3) in subsection (c), by inserting “Termination.—” after “(c)”; 
        (4) in subsection (d), by inserting “Notice to Department of the Interior.—” after “(d)”; and 
        (5) in subsection (e), by inserting “Disposition of Consideration.—” after “(e)”.  
    (c) Conforming Repeal.—Section 2669 of such title is repealed. 
    (d) Clerical Amendment.—The table of sections at the beginning of chapter 159 of such title is amended by striking the item related to section 2669.

fable.w: The section makes technical and consolidating amendments to the Secretary's authority to grant easements, plus stylistic headings and a conforming repeal. The tempting reading is that the 'Notice to Department of the Interior' heading or the mention of states, citizens and corporations as easement recipients signals outside involvement. That fails because notice to Interior is intra-federal, and the recipients language is being struck and concerns who receives easements, not consultation on a federal decision. Nothing here provides for comment, a hearing, an advisory body, rulemaking, or a right to sue.
fable.s: by inserting “Notice to Department of the Interior.—” after “(d)”

opus.w: This section only makes technical, stylistic and conforming amendments to the military easement statute (10 U.S.C. 2668) and repeals section 2669. The one procedural item is a heading for notice to the Department of the Interior, which is communication between federal agencies, not participation. The struck reference to states, political subdivisions and private parties concerns who may receive easements, not anyone being consulted, so no one outside the federal government takes part in a federal decision.
opus.s: (4) in subsection (d), by inserting “Notice to Department of the Interior.—” after “(d)”; and
opus.b: The tempting reading is "Yes," because the text mentions "a State, Commonwealth, or possession, or political subdivision thereof" and a "Notice to Department of the Interior." That reading fails on both points. The reference to states is being *struck*: it only describes who may receive easements, and it creates no consultation. The Department of the Interior is a federal agency, so notifying it stays inside the federal government.

qwen_chat.w: The section primarily contains stylistic and conforming amendments to existing law regarding easements. The only potential interaction mentioned is a 'Notice to Department of the Interior,' but the Department of the Interior is a federal agency, making this intra-governmental coordination rather than participation by an outside party. There is no requirement for public comment, advisory committees with non-federal members, or consultation with states, tribes, or the public.
qwen_chat.s: (4) in subsection (d), by inserting “Notice to Department of the Interior.—” after “(d)”; and
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the amendment to subsection (d) inserting "Notice to Department of the Interior" implies a consultation or coordination process with an outside entity. However, the Department of the Interior is a federal agency, so any interaction with it is intra-governmental and does not constitute participation by an outside party. Furthermore, the section primarily consists of stylistic and conforming amendments to existing statutory text regarding easements, without introducing new mechanisms for public comment, advisory boards with non-federal members, or consultation with states/tribes/public.
